posts.quote: Some days the whole plan is a warm drink and not being found.
posts.caption:
The best seat in my house is behind the bookshelf, and nobody knows it.

I found it in March, when the house was loud and I needed eleven quiet minutes. Since then I've added a blanket, a good mug and a lamp with a soft bulb. From there I can hear everything and be asked nothing. Someone called my name twice yesterday. I held very still, the way deer do. It worked until the dog gave me away. I came out with my tea still warm and a new respect for furniture.

Some days the plan really is just the plan.
posts.first: My sister walked right past the armchair this morning and said the house felt oddly peaceful. I sipped my tea in silence. The dog looked straight at me, which was the closest thing to betrayal I've had all week. She left without a word and I stayed put.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun curled up in an armchair behind a tall bookshelf holding a steaming mug, a throw blanket on her knees. Text in the speech bubble at the top reads: Some days the whole plan is a warm drink and not being found.

posts.quote: I said my date of birth out loud to an automated phone voice in the cereal aisle. Three strangers now know I'm fifty-three, and one of them nodded.
posts.caption: The pharmacy line wanted my birthday and it wanted it clearly. The microphone and I disagreed about the year twice. By the third try the whole aisle was invested.
posts.first: The man who nodded was holding a bag of oatmeal and looked like he'd done the same thing recently. We didn't speak. I took a different aisle for the rest of the trip, out of respect for both of us.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun holding her phone out in a grocery store cereal aisle while three shoppers look on, a basket on her arm holding a wine bottle and cereal. Text in the speech bubble reads: I said my date of birth out loud to an automated phone voice in the cereal aisle. Three strangers now know I'm fifty-three, and one of them nodded.

posts.quote: I swapped the evening news for a baking competition. So far nobody has been indicted over a soggy bottom.
posts.caption: It began as a ten-minute break from the headlines. Then a retired schoolteacher in a floral apron wept over a collapsed sponge, and the judge handed her a hug instead of a verdict. I watched four episodes. I now know the difference between a proof and a prove, and I have strong feelings about lamination. Nobody raised their voice. The worst thing that happened was a meringue. I slept like a person with nothing on her conscience. I'm told there is a finale, and I plan to be there.
posts.first: Last night the contestants made a cake shaped like a lighthouse and it leaned. The whole tent went quiet, and a man said a very soft word. I felt that in my chest. I've never baked anything taller than a muffin and I'm already on his side.
posts.alt: Painted illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun curled up on a couch under a blanket with a glass of red wine and a bowl of popcorn, watching a television showing a baking tent with pies. Text at the top reads: I swapped the evening news for a baking competition. Text at the bottom reads: So far nobody has been indicted over a soggy bottom.

posts.quote: My refrigerator texted me that the door was open. I was standing next to it, looking at it, with the door open.
posts.caption: The notification said Door Open, in the voice of a small anxious bureaucrat. I looked at the phone. I looked at the refrigerator. I looked at the light inside, which was on, and at my hand, which was on the handle. I closed the door. The phone then thanked me. I don't remember agreeing to a relationship with this appliance, but here we are, exchanging updates. It once told me the freezer was warm, and I told it I could relate. It did not reply, which I respected.
posts.first: I stood in the kitchen after that, holding the leftover soup, and said thank you to the room. The refrigerator hummed. It sounded fine with how things stood. I put the soup back, closed the door gently and went to the couch.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun holding up her phone with a flat unimpressed look, a glass of red wine in her other hand, next to an open refrigerator door on a plain cream background. Text beside her reads: My refrigerator texted me that the door was open. I was standing next to it, looking at it, with the door open.

posts.quote: A neighbor said good morning. I said what, then huh. Technically that's three greetings and I'm counting them all.
posts.caption: He was being polite and I was being deaf in two languages. We both walked away feeling we'd made a good effort.
posts.first: He waved again from his driveway ten minutes later and I waved back with real enthusiasm, as if that settled everything. It did, mostly. I'm now practicing a clean good morning in the mirror.
posts.alt: Comic panel illustration with a thick black border of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun on a front porch holding a glass of red wine and cupping her hand to her ear toward a smiling neighbor across a low fence. Text at the top reads: A neighbor said good morning. Text at the bottom reads: I said what, then huh. Technically that's three greetings and I'm counting them all.

posts.quote: I spent fifty minutes on the phone to dispute a $4.99 charge. I won. It cost me about thirty dollars of afternoon.
posts.caption: Four dollars and ninety-nine cents is not a number that should require a plan, but I made one anyway. I had my statement, a pen and a posture. I was transferred twice and apologized to once. A very nice man named Marcus said he could see the problem and that it would take five to seven business days. I thanked him as though he had cured something. By the end the notepad was full of doodles and my tea was cold. It is the principle, and also a small, quiet victory I'll be thinking about all week.
posts.first: The refund showed up on Thursday morning as a line of text on my phone. I read it twice and set the phone down gently. I told the dog about it, and he stayed asleep. That's the kind of support I've come to expect.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun at a kitchen table with a phone on speaker, a scribbled notepad and a glass of red wine, raising one fist in victory. Text in the speech bubble at the top reads: I spent fifty minutes on the phone to dispute a $4.99 charge. I won. It cost me about thirty dollars of afternoon.

posts.quote: I found a cassette tape in a drawer. I own nothing that plays it. I put it back, because some things you keep on principle.
posts.caption: The label is in my own handwriting from a Tuesday in 1991. I held it for a while. Then it went back under the batteries and the takeout menus, where it belongs.
posts.first: The handwriting says Songs For The Drive, with two underlines. I have no idea what's on it and I'd like to leave it that way. The drawer closes a little harder now, in a good way.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun kneeling by an open bedroom dresser drawer, holding up a cassette tape with a wistful smile, a glass of red wine on the dresser. Text in the speech bubble reads: I found a cassette tape in a drawer. I own nothing that plays it. I put it back, because some things you keep on principle.

posts.quote: A pot of tea, a heavy sweater, and rain that doesn't need anything from me. October is doing its best work.
posts.first: I put the kettle on at four and nothing else. The windows fogged a little, the way they do. My sweater is the color of oatmeal and has a hole near the cuff that I've never fixed. It felt like a full day, and it was only Thursday.

posts.quote: Seventy degrees in October is just the weather apologizing.
posts.caption:
Seventy degrees in late October feels like being let off a hook I didn't know I was on.

I had the heavy sweater out, the blankets sorted and a list of excuses for staying in until April. Then the porch thermometer said seventy and the whole plan fell apart. I carried the swing cushions out of the closet, dusted off the pumpkins and sat. Sun on my knees, a light breeze, no scarf. A neighbor walked by in a sweater, sweating politely, and we both pretended it was normal. I'm choosing to accept the apology with no follow-up questions.

Winter can wait its turn.
posts.first: I sat out there long enough to watch two more neighbors walk by in sweaters. One of them said, enjoy it. I said I'm trying. Then I sat very still so the weather wouldn't notice me and change its mind. It's a delicate arrangement and I'm not touching it.
posts.alt: Comic panel illustration with a thick black border of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun on a sunny porch swing with a glass of red wine, orange leaves and pumpkins around the steps. Text at the top reads: Seventy degrees in October is just the weather apologizing.

posts.quote: The couch has a dent in it that is the exact shape of my entire fall.
posts.caption:
The couch has been taking notes on me since September.

It started small. One cushion, one blanket, one spot by the lamp. By October the dent had a shape, and the shape had my name on it. I've tried fluffing it, flipping it and rotating the cushion, and it springs right back to me like a loyal pet. Guests sit on the far end without being told. The dog naps in the warm part when I'm out. I'm not sure whether I broke the couch or the couch trained me, and I've decided to call it a partnership.

We're very happy together.
posts.first: My cousin sat in the dent at Thanksgiving last year and sank like she'd been pulled in. She said, who sits here? Everyone looked at me. I said that's a guest seat, in a very calm voice. She moved to the chair. The dent waited, patient as ever.
posts.alt: Painted illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun sprawled on a dented couch under a plaid blanket with a glass of red wine, autumn light through a window. Text at the top reads: The couch has a dent in it that is the exact shape of my entire fall.

posts.quote: The self-checkout said there was an unexpected item in the bagging area. It was my purse. We've been together eleven years.
posts.caption: The machine wanted to know what I'd added. I told it, with feeling. It asked me to wait for assistance, so we waited together, the purse and I.
posts.first: The attendant came over, scanned her badge and cleared the screen without a word. She glanced at my purse and said, I get it. We nodded at each other like people who've both had a long relationship with a handbag. I bagged my groceries and left with my dignity mostly packed.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration with a thick black comic border of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun and a pencil in it, reading glasses on her forehead, standing at a self-checkout lane with one hand resting on a brown leather purse on the bagging scale and a deadpan stare at the screen showing a red warning triangle, a shopping basket with a wine bottle at her feet. Text at the top reads: The self-checkout said there was an unexpected item in the bagging area. Text at the bottom reads: It was my purse. We've been together eleven years.

posts.quote: I bought a plant labeled impossible to kill. We are in week three of a standoff.
posts.caption: The tag said it thrives on neglect, and I took that as a personal challenge in the opposite direction. I watered it on a schedule. I moved it to the window, then away from the window, then to a different window. It dropped three leaves on Tuesday, in what I can only call a statement. I've read the tag again. It still says impossible. At this point one of us is lying, and the plant has the better track record. I'm giving it another week and a little more light.
posts.first: My neighbor, who grows tomatoes in a bathtub, looked at it over the fence and said it just needs to feel unobserved. I now walk past it with my eyes on the floor. It has put out one small green leaf. I'm not going to mention it.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun holding a droopy yellow-leafed potted plant at arm's length with a suspicious squint, a glass of red wine in her other hand, on a plain cream background. Text beside her reads: I bought a plant labeled impossible to kill. We are in week three of a standoff.

posts.quote: A package came. I watched through the blinds until the truck left, then opened the door. I'm not hiding. I'm pacing myself.
posts.caption: The driver was friendly and there was no need for a hello. I waited a respectful two minutes. The package and I were then introduced.
posts.first: It turned out to be a set of drawer organizers. I carried them upstairs like a prize and then sat in the quiet for a while, delighted with myself and the rest of my afternoon.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun crouched in a front hallway peeking through window blinds with a glass of red wine in her hand, a cardboard package on the doorstep outside. Text in the speech bubble at the top reads: A package came. I watched through the blinds until the truck left, then opened the door. I'm not hiding. I'm pacing myself.

posts.quote: The leaf blower next door started at 7:02 on a Saturday. I've been awake since 7:03, and so have my opinions.
posts.caption: I'd set no alarm. That was the whole point of Saturday. At 7:02 the blower started up like a small airport, and by 7:03 I'd planned a speech. I lay there and edited it. I considered a note, a plate of cookies with a message and moving to a different zip code. Instead I made coffee and stood at the window in my robe, glaring with love. He finished in eleven minutes. The yard looked wonderful, which made it worse. I've decided to forgive him by Tuesday, once the leaves are back.
posts.first: He waved at me when he was done, a big cheerful wave with a gloved hand. I raised my mug at him, the way you'd salute a small parade. We're fine. We'll always be fine. I'm just going to be tired about it.
posts.alt: Painted illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun sitting upright in bed with wild bedhead, glaring at a bedroom window where a neighbor blows orange leaves with a leaf blower, a coffee mug on the nightstand. Text at the top reads: The leaf blower next door started at 7:02 on a Saturday. Text at the bottom reads: I've been awake since 7:03, and so have my opinions.

posts.quote: I asked my stylist for something low maintenance. She looked at me, then at my hair, then at me again.
posts.caption: I'd practiced the sentence in the car. Low maintenance, just something easy, nothing fussy. She took the pencil out of my hair and held it up between two fingers, slowly, like evidence. We both looked at it. Then she began a short, kind speech about expectations that I mostly agreed with. The cut was great. It takes eight minutes and no tools, which, for me, is a miracle with a price. I left the salon feeling lighter and slightly seen. The pencil went back in on the drive home.
posts.first: Three days later the haircut is still holding. I washed it, tossed my head once and went out the door. It felt like cheating. I'm told this is what it's like for other people, and I'd like to thank them.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun and a pencil in her hair, sitting in a salon chair in a black cape and looking at a stylist's reflection in the mirror. Text in the speech bubble reads: I asked my stylist for something low maintenance. She looked at me, then at my hair, then at me again.

posts.quote: I don't need a spa day. I need a locked bathroom door and eleven minutes.
posts.caption: The lock on my bathroom door is the best money I ever spent on a house. It clicks like a vault. Nobody has ever knocked in under four minutes, and I count.
posts.first: Last week I had nine of my eleven minutes when the knocking started. It was the dog, scratching, which I counted as a technicality. I stayed on the edge of the tub, finished my chapter and flushed for credibility. Some victories are small, and they're mine.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun sitting calmly on the edge of a bathtub in a bathroom with a locked door, a lit candle and a glass of red wine nearby. Text in the speech bubble reads: I don't need a spa day. I need a locked bathroom door and eleven minutes.
